data: Status: the parser (M1) is released in v0.2.0, the lowering (M2) and the type system of core in v0.3.0; the rest is planned. This page is the design the bibliography recommends. Where the bibliography says a point is unmeasured, this page says so. The lowering section below records what was built.
data.base-run-it-unchanged#Base: run it uncha: Base is bootstrapped by evaluating base/boot.jl and then the file list of base/Base_compiler.jl and base/Base.jl. The recommendation is to run Base unchanged through the interpreter, at build time, and ship the resulting heap as an image. Only two things are ported to Go: the builtins, intrinsics and foreigncall targets; and hot leaf methods after profiling, replaced by method overrides registered in Go (same signature, same results, a test comparing both). Base is 140 705 lines whose semantics are the definition of Julia: a native rewrite would diverge, and every Base fix upstream would have to be ported twice.
data.lowering-the-design-as-planned-julialowe: src/julia-syntax.scm (+ macroexpand.scm, ast.scm) JuliaLowering/src language femtolisp Scheme, pattern-matching macros Julia, plain functions over a SyntaxGraph size 5 779 + 733 + 568 lines 13 940 lines status default in the system image but off by default provenance line numbers only byte-precise The recommendation is to port JuliaLowering: it is Julia with explicit data structures, closer to Go than Scheme pattern rewriting; it is MIT; it carries the provenance a notebook needs for file:line errors; and upstream is moving to it. The risk is that its coverage is not measured: if it lowers much less than Base, M2 becomes a port of julia-syntax.scm. The oracle in all cases is Meta.lower on the reference binary, compared on CodeInfo after renumbering slots and SSA values.
data.lowering-what-v030-built-m2#Lowering: wh:
The risk below came true in the sense the bibliography allowed: julia 1.12.6 lowers with the femtolisp front end by default and JuliaLowering is not part of the reference’s Meta.lower, so M2 is a port of julia-syntax.scm, the code that produces the goldens. The lower package ports julia-syntax.scm, macroexpand.scm, ast.scm and match.scm, pass by pass: expand-forms, resolve-scopes, analyze-variables!, closure-convert, linearize, then renumbering into CodeInfo. Hygiene (resolve-expansion-vars, rename-symbolic-labels) is ported too.
lower.NewState().Lower(ex) is Meta.lower of a macro-expanded top-level form: an Expr(:thunk, CodeInfo), an atom, or Expr(:error); one State per module, in file order. Macro expansion runs user code, so it stays with the caller, as in julia. Outputs are compared with julia’s field by field, modulo gensym numbering (the counters live for a whole julia session, so two sessions differ).
measured on forms identical to julia corpus (share/julia: base, Compiler, stdlib, test), 1191 files 53 997 53 997 (1191/1191 files) lowering snippets 124 124 macro-made toplevels still in hygienic scopes 48 48 built expressions (error paths, rare heads) 477 477 deparse vs julia --lisp 119 119 front-end functions vs julia --lisp 151 151 Statement coverage is 100%, every expectation coming from julia. Lower refuses trees deeper than lower.MaxDepth (1000) with lower.ErrLimit, and FuzzLower runs on every pull request. Known gap: a Float64 inside a lowering error message makes Lower return lower.ErrUnsupported.
data.parser-port-juliasyntax#Parser: port Jul: JuliaSyntax is the default parser since Julia 1.10, and Base itself loads it. Bootstrapping forces a native parser. Until Base loads it, Julia parses base/*.jl with the femtolisp parser in C. A Go VM has no femtolisp, so it needs a Go parser before any Julia runs; running JuliaSyntax through the interpreter is not an option for the first files. JuliaSyntax is a hand-written recursive-descent parser over a token stream with a separate green tree, and a module that builds Expr. It ports line by line to Go, as rbgo’s parser was built. Oracle: the real JuliaSyntax.parseall(Expr, …) on every file of base/, stdlib/, test/ and the JuliaSyntax test corpus, compared as serialised Expr trees.
data.parser-usage-v020#Parser: usage (v0.2.0):
syntax.ParseAll(src, filename) in go-embedded-julia/julia returns the same Expr as julia’s Meta.parseall, including julia’s error Expr: the statements before the first error, then Expr(:error) or Expr(:incomplete) with the formatted ParseError.
e := syntax.ParseAll([]byte("f(x) = x^2 + 1"), "cell.jl") serialises to
(:toplevel {L 1 :"cell.jl"} (:"=" (:call :f :x) (:block {L 1 :"cell.jl"} (:call :"+" (:call :"^" :x 2) 1)))) Parsing is bounded (64 MiB, depth 4000) and ParseAllLimits returns an error rather than an Expr on failure. Known gap: on a few malformed inputs JuliaSyntax itself throws and julia falls back to femtolisp, which is not ported; there ParseAll returns Expr(:error) and ParseAllLimits an error wrapping syntax.ErrParserFailed.
data.released-so-far-the-core-package-v030#Re:
core — Julia’s type objects, apply_type, and subtyping (a port of jltypes.c and subtype.c of 1.12.6, without intersection): identical to julia on 20 000 random pairs and 4 902 cases from test/subtype.jl.
FuzzSubtype runs on every pull request. Subtyping is 1.37× slower than julia’s jl_subtype on one core (3.26 ms against 2.39 ms for the 20 000 pairs, best of 7 interleaved rounds, load 4.4–6.6, 2026-11-01), an open defect: #20. It was 1.43× before the query environments were pooled (v0.9.1), which halved the allocations (−51%, −66% of bytes); the time gain of the pooling alone is not confirmed at low load.
data.released-so-far-the-interp-package-v060-: interp — a port of julia 1.12.6’s src/interpreter.c that runs lowered code over Core. interp.New().NewSession().Eval(src) parses, lowers and runs a cell; interp.Repr shows the value as julia does. struct and abstract type definitions (v0.7.0) run through the builtins lowering calls, which build the default outer and inner constructors as jl_ctor_def does; calling a type dispatches on its constructors, and user-defined outer constructors join them. Methods with where clauses (v0.8.0) dispatch with static parameters (e.g. f(x::T) where {T<:Integer} = T), through the TypeVar and UnionAll constructors of boot.jl:335-338, built in Go until boot.jl runs. Structs and abstract types with parameters (v0.9.0): Q(1) infers Q{Int64}, Q{Integer}(1) runs the inner constructor, a parameter no field constrains gets no outer constructor (as jl_ctor_def decides), constructor signatures keep the called type first as in julia’s one method table, and a type argument dispatches as Type{X}. Macros are expanded before lowering (v0.10.0), a port of jl_expand_macros: a macro call runs the macro’s method with __source__ and __module__, hygiene goes through the hygienic-scope that lower resolves, nested and recursive calls are expanded in turn, quotes go through lower.Backquote, and a self-expanding macro raises StackOverflowError. Boot (v0.11.0): Core is defined by julia 1.12.6’s own base/boot.jl, unmodified and embedded; vm.Boot() evaluates all 363 forms in Core, then runs post_boot_hooks (jltypes.c:3909-3968), so builtins raise boot.jl’s exception types and an error in an included file is a LoadError. After Boot, vm.CoreSession().Eval(src) runs code in Core; Boot is opt-in and interp.New().NewSession().Eval is unchanged. Ported from julia’s C sources for it: the types jl_init_types creates (real layouts for the IR nodes, GenericMemory, GenericMemoryRef and Array, plus AddrSpace and Core.CPU), module expressions with relative using .M / import ..M paths, the builtins _primitivetype, setfield!, invokelatest and invoke_in_world, getfield of types and AST nodes, the intrinsics trunc_int, sext_int, zext_int, bitcast, shl_int, lshr_int and ashr_int, and ccall to Go shims keyed by the C function’s name (an unknown name is ErrUnsupported when the call runs). include reads only VM.Sources, never the host’s filesystem, and an include that nests without end raises StackOverflowError. Not yet: arrays as values programs use (an Expr’s args), and Base. Boot has no julia counterpart to measure against, since julia’s Core comes from its system image. Core has the built-in types, the exception and AST types of boot.jl and jltypes.c (with the QuoteNode, LineNumberNode and Expr constructors), 26 builtins and the integer and float intrinsics. 97 Core-only programs show the same value in Go and julia 1.12.6; 100% statement coverage; fuzzed (FuzzEval). Not yet: Base (+, println, a.b, constructor arguments that need convert, macros that use esc or Base’s macros), splatting anything but a tuple or a simple vector (it calls Base.iterate), redefining a struct that has parameters (it needs Base.getproperty), const and atomic fields, arrays, finally; the speed against julia’s interpreter is not measured yet.
data.risks-the-plan-names#Risks the plan name: Subtyping and specificity diverging silently from subtype.c. JuliaLowering’s coverage of Base, not yet measured. Interpretive speed: Base’s generic code relies on inlining and specialisation. Mitigations are dispatch caches keyed by concrete argument types, fast paths for intrinsic-only methods, and Go overrides for measured hot leaves. Pointers and unsafe_*: a pointer must be modelled as a buffer and an offset into Go memory, checked on every access, so that a malformed unsafe_load raises instead of corrupting the VM. Security: notebook and playground cells are untrusted. The plan fuzzes the parser and the image reader, and bounds recursion depth, allocation sizes and regex steps. Unicode version must match utf8proc’s, or test/unicode.jl diverges. Upstream moves fast: the sources were read at 1.15.0-DEV; the plan pins a release and tracks the next one deliberately.
data.runtime-in-go#Runtime in Go: C file (lines) Go component jltypes.c 4 728, datatype.c 3 200 type objects: DataType, UnionAll, Union, TypeVar, Vararg, layout, type cache; field layout must match for sizeof, fieldoffset, reinterpret subtype.c 7 737 issubtype, type_intersection, morespecific: the hardest part, with test/subtype.jl (3 666 lines) and test/specificity.jl as oracles gf.c 6 567, typemap.c 1 795, method.c 1 538 method tables, dispatch cache, world ages, ambiguity builtins.c 3 161 the builtins (63 in julia 1.12.6; 83 on 1.15-DEV, where the line counts were taken), each a Go function runtime_intrinsics.c 1 862 the intrinsics (93 in julia 1.12.6; 94 on 1.15-DEV, where the line counts were taken) interpreter.c 1 118, toplevel.c 1 020 the interpreter over CodeInfo and top-level eval module.c 2 504 modules, bindings, binding partitions genericmemory.c 631, array.c 324 Memory{T} and MemoryRef; Array is defined in Julia on top task.c, partr.c, gc-*.c, signals-*.c a goroutine per Task with a hand-off channel (one runs at a time, as in Julia’s single-threaded scheduler); the Go GC; no signals staticdata.c 5 103 the interpreter’s own image format; not a port of sys.ji subtype.c is where a reimplementation diverges silently (the diagonal rule, Union distribution, Vararg, TypeVar bounds). The plan is to port it statement by statement rather than from the paper.
data.the-image-is-the-start-up#The image is t:
Julia without a system image evaluates boot.jl and all of Base at start. Through an interpreter that is 140 705 lines, plus the 36 867-line Compiler if inference is interpreted: minutes, not seconds. So the build runs the bootstrap once, natively, and writes the resulting heap (modules, bindings, types, method tables, lowered CodeInfo, interned symbols, the _return_type cache, constant data such as Unicode tables) to a versioned binary image, embedded with go:embed or fetched next to the WebAssembly module. This is Julia’s own design (sys.ji) without native code.
The image size is unknown until M4. The start-up budget to hold is that image deserialisation stays under the Ruby core’s 2.3 s on the same machine (a figure the plan reports but did not re-measure); per-module images (LinearAlgebra only when using LinearAlgebra runs) are the lever if it is not met.
data.the-interpreter#The interpreter: Its shape follows JuliaInterpreter: a Frame with locals (slots) and SSA values, a program counter over CodeInfo.code, GotoNode, GotoIfNot and ReturnNode as control flow, and :enter and :leave as an exception-handler stack. JuliaInterpreter is the evidence that lowered IR is directly executable for the whole of Base. Its limit is also the port’s: it hands foreigncall and llvmcall to compiled wrappers, which is exactly where the Go port needs its shim table instead.
data.the-notebook-bridge#The notebook bridge: The Ruby cells of go-notebook define the contract to copy: one shared interpreter for all cells of the language; only variables cross; a cell defines the top-level names it assigns and uses the names it reads first, taken from the language’s own parser; errors are reported at the notebook line. The plan proposes a Julia to Go value table (integers at their width, BigInt as *big.Int, BigFloat as *big.Float, String as string, arrays as *ndarray.Array sharing the same buffer with column-major strides kept) and a go-scikit/julia package modelled on go-scikit/ruby. Julia is column-major and go-ndarray is NumPy-style strided, so go-ndarray must accept Fortran strides without copying: the plan lists that as unconfirmed.
data.the-pipeline#The pipeline: source ──JuliaSyntax (Go port)──▶ Expr ──macroexpand──▶ Expr ──JuliaLowering (Go port)──▶ CodeInfo ──▶ toplevel eval (toplevel.c semantics) ──▶ method tables ──call──▶ dispatch (gf.c, typemap.c, subtype.c) ──▶ interpreter over lowered IR (interpreter.c semantics) ──▶ builtins (63 in julia 1.12.6), intrinsics (93 in julia 1.12.6), foreigncall shim table This is the pipeline Julia’s own developer documentation describes (eval.md), minus the code-generation step. Julia already interprets some top-level code instead of compiling it, and “the bulk of the work to interpret code is handled by eval in interpreter.c”. The port makes the interpreted branch the only one.
data.type-inference-only-where-bases-results-:
Base calls inference for results, not only for speed: Base._return_type is used by promote_op, and through it by map, broadcast and collect on empty inputs and by accumulate. map(x -> x + 1, Int[]) returning Vector{Int} and not Vector{Any} is an observable result. Two options:
interpret Compiler/src (36 867 lines) itself, lazily, only when _return_type is called: correct by construction, slow; a small Go abstract interpreter over the same lowered IR: fast, and wrong in the corners. The recommendation is option 1 first, with a per-signature cache that is part of the image; option 2 only if measurement shows the notebook waiting on it, and then checked against option 1.
data.what-julia-is-made-of#What Julia is made: Part Path Lines Role for a Go port C/C++ runtime and codegen src/*.{c,cpp,h} 169 453 a specification; the LLVM half is dropped its semantic core subtype.c, gf.c, jltypes.c, datatype.c, builtins.c, module.c, … (15 files) 36 477 what must be re-expressed in Go Base, in Julia base/**/*.jl (202 files) 140 705 run as is through the interpreter type inference and optimiser Compiler/src (41 files) 36 867 not needed for speed; see below parser, in Julia JuliaSyntax/src (18 files) 11 326 port to Go lowering, in Julia JuliaLowering/src (17 files) 13 940 port to Go legacy front end, femtolisp src/*.scm (11 files) 10 622 oracle and fallback JuliaInterpreter src/*.jl (12 files) 6 943 design reference test suite test/**/*.jl (297 files) 130 413 oracle The lowered IR has 12 node types and 30 Expr heads: that is the whole instruction set an interpreter must execute. Julia’s own C interpreter over it is 1 118 lines.

data: Status: planned. No code has been translated yet. This page records what the plan allows, and the rules it will hold to.
data.inside-base-with-their-own-licence#Insid: base/ryu/* is under the Boost licence, and base/special/rem_pio2.jl and base/special/hyperbolic.jl carry an FDLIBM notice. Both run as Julia through the interpreter, and the notices travel with the image.
data.libraries-base-calls-replaced-not-linked: Library Licence What the plan does GMP LGPL-3.0-or-later or GPL-2.0-or-later not linked, not translated: replaced by math/big and go-bignum, written from the documented semantics, not from its source MPFR LGPL-3.0-or-later the same PCRE BSD-3-Clause replaced by a front end on go-ruby-regexp utf8proc MIT replaced by Go’s unicode and x/text/unicode/norm libuv MIT replaced by Go’s os, net and time OpenBLAS and LAPACK BSD-3-Clause replaced by go-ndarray’s linalg
data.the-gpl-parts-to-avoid#The GPL parts to:
SuiteSparse’s libumfpack, libspqr and librbio are GPL-2.0-or-later, and libcholmod is LGPL-2.1-or-later and GPL-2.0-or-later. They back SparseArrays, an external standard library, whose \ on sparse matrices goes to UMFPACK and CHOLMOD. A Go port of SparseArrays must use the fleet’s sparse solvers (go-sparse) and must not read SuiteSparse source. Julia’s stock build includes these libraries (USE_GPL_LIBS ?= 1 in Make.inc), so they are a thing to keep out, not a thing that is absent.
FFTW is GPL but is not in Julia’s tree: FFTW.jl is a registry package, and the plan serves its API over go-fft instead.
data.what-may-be-translated-to-go-with-the-no:
Julia is MIT, and Julia’s THIRDPARTY.md states that the language “consists of the compiler (the contents of src/), most of the standard library (base/ and stdlib/)”. So these are all MIT and may be translated to Go with the notice kept:
Source Licence src/ (the C runtime) MIT base/, stdlib/ MIT JuliaSyntax/ MIT JuliaLowering/ MIT JuliaInterpreter.jl MIT LinearAlgebra.jl, Statistics.jl MIT src/flisp (femtolisp) BSD-3-Clause dSFMT BSD-3-Clause; may be translated

Status: in development. M0 (oracle harness), M1 (parser) and M2 (lowering) are done, released as v0.3.0 (2026-10-28) of go-embedded-julia/julia, against julia 1.12.6. M3 is in progress (v0.4.0, v0.5.0, v0.6.0, v0.7.0, v0.8.0, v0.9.0, v0.10.0, v0.11.0); M4 to M7 are planned.
M2 in numbers: the lower package ports julia 1.12.6’s femtolisp front end (julia-syntax.scm, macroexpand.scm, ast.scm, match.scm). lower.NewState().Lower(ex) is Meta.lower of a macro-expanded top-level form, compared with julia field by field, modulo gensym numbering. It is identical on 53 997 of 53 997 forms of julia 1.12.6’s share/julia tree (base, Compiler, stdlib, test; 1191 of 1191 files), 124 of 124 lowering snippets, 48 of 48 hygienic-scope forms and 477 of 477 built expressions (error paths, rare heads); deparse matches julia --lisp on 119 of 119 forms and the front-end functions on 151 of 151 calls. Statement coverage is 100%. Lower refuses trees deeper than lower.MaxDepth (1000) and FuzzLower runs on every pull request. Known gap: a Float64 inside a lowering error message makes Lower return lower.ErrUnsupported.
M3 so far: core — Julia’s type objects, apply_type, and subtyping (a port of jltypes.c and subtype.c of 1.12.6, without intersection): identical to julia on 20 000 random pairs and 4 902 cases from test/subtype.jl; and method specificity (jl_type_morespecific, v0.4.0), identical to Base.morespecific on the same corpus. core/dispatch (v0.5.0): method tables with world ages, and the method a call with concrete argument types runs, with its static parameters: identical to julia’s which and dispatch environment on 9 000 calls over 1 500 random method tables (4 675 method choices, 1 968 with static parameters, 87 ambiguities). interp (v0.6.0 to v0.11.0): a port of julia 1.12.6’s src/interpreter.c that runs lowered code over Core (interp.New().NewSession().Eval(src), interp.Repr); v0.7.0 runs struct and abstract type definitions with julia’s default constructors (jl_ctor_def) and user-defined outer constructors, and calling a type dispatches on its constructors. v0.8.0 dispatches methods with where clauses with static parameters (e.g. f(x::T) where {T<:Integer} = T), through the TypeVar and UnionAll constructors of boot.jl:335-338, built in Go until boot.jl runs. v0.9.0 runs structs and abstract types with parameters (struct Q{T}, abstract type A{T}): Q(1) infers Q{Int64}, Q{Integer}(1) runs the inner constructor, a parameter no field constrains gets no outer constructor (as jl_ctor_def decides), constructor signatures keep the called type first as in julia’s one method table, and a type argument dispatches as Type{X}. v0.10.0 expands macros, a port of jl_expand_macros: a macro call runs the macro’s method with __source__ and __module__, hygiene goes through the hygienic-scope that lower resolves, nested and recursive macro calls are expanded in turn, quotes go through lower.Backquote, and a self-expanding macro raises StackOverflowError. v0.11.0 defines Core by julia 1.12.6’s own base/boot.jl, unmodified and embedded: vm.Boot() evaluates its 363 forms in Core, then runs post_boot_hooks (jltypes.c:3909-3968), so builtins raise boot.jl’s exception types and an error in an included file is a LoadError. After Boot, vm.CoreSession().Eval(src) runs code in Core; Boot is opt-in, and interp.New().NewSession().Eval is unchanged. Ported from julia’s C sources for it: the types jl_init_types creates (with real layouts for the IR nodes, GenericMemory, GenericMemoryRef and Array, plus AddrSpace and Core.CPU); module expressions and relative using .M / import ..M paths; the builtins _primitivetype, setfield!, invokelatest and invoke_in_world; getfield of types (DataType, TypeName, TypeVar, UnionAll, Union, Vararg) and of AST nodes; the intrinsics trunc_int, sext_int, zext_int, bitcast, shl_int, lshr_int and ashr_int; and ccall to Go shims keyed by the C function’s name (an unknown name is ErrUnsupported when the call runs). Display fixes, checked against julia 1.12.6: Float32 (1.0f0, NaN32), Char (escapes, malformed bytes, \u/\U) and nested modules (Main.L.B). include reads only VM.Sources (julia’s embedded sources by default), never the host’s filesystem, and an include that nests without end raises StackOverflowError. Not yet in v0.11.0: arrays as values programs use (an Expr’s args), and Base. Speed: Boot has no julia counterpart to measure against, since julia’s Core comes from its system image. Core has the built-in types, the exception and AST types of boot.jl and jltypes.c (with the QuoteNode, LineNumberNode and Expr constructors), 26 builtins (the six type-definition builtins and fieldtype are new in v0.7.0, _typevar in v0.8.0, _expr and _apply_iterate in v0.10.0) and the integer and float intrinsics. Checked: 97 Core-only programs show the same value in Go and julia 1.12.6; 100% statement coverage; fuzzed (FuzzEval). Not yet: type intersection, and with it the interference sets julia 1.12 uses to order matches; Base (+, println, a.b, and constructor arguments that need convert, macros that use esc or Base’s macros), splatting anything but a tuple or a simple vector (it calls Base.iterate), redefining a struct that has parameters (it needs Base.getproperty), const and atomic fields, arrays, finally, and the remaining builtins and intrinsics. Speed: subtyping is 1.37× slower than julia’s jl_subtype on one core (3.26 ms against 2.39 ms for the 20 000 pairs, best of 7 interleaved rounds, load 4.4–6.6, 2026-11-01), an open defect (#20); pooling the query environments (v0.9.1) halved the allocations (−51%); the speed of the interpreter against julia’s is not measured yet.
M1 in numbers: a Go port of JuliaSyntax 29ec5226f7b1, the version julia 1.12.6 ships. Tokens, green trees and Expr are identical to julia’s on 1191 of 1191 files of julia 1.12.6’s share/julia tree (base, Compiler, stdlib, test; 18.5 MB) and on 976 of 976 golden snippets. On one core the corpus parses in 0.98 s against 1.39 s for julia’s Meta.parseall (0.70x). Parsing is bounded (64 MiB, depth 4000) and fuzzed; coverage is 100%, tested natively on amd64/arm64/386, under qemu on riscv64/loong64/ppc64le/s390x/arm, compiled for every GOOS/GOARCH, and run on wasip1 under wazero. Known gap: on a few malformed inputs (import. .., import. ...x, 0:0:<) JuliaSyntax itself throws and julia falls back to the femtolisp parser, which is not ported: there ParseAll returns Expr(:error) and ParseAllLimits returns an error wrapping syntax.ErrParserFailed.
Effort is on the roadmap’s scale: S days, M weeks, L months, XL several months. M3 and M4 dominate; in total the effort is on the order of the rbgo effort, plus a parser and a lowering pass that rbgo did not need in this form.
data.how-conformance-is-measured#How conforma:
Julia’s test suite is written with the Test standard library, and test/choosetests.jl lists the test names. The harness:
runs each listed file under the reference julia and under the interpreter, one file per worker process with a timeout, each with a Test reporter that emits one JSON record per @test (file, line, expression, pass, fail, error or broken); compares records, not totals: a test passing in both, failing only in the interpreter (a defect), or failing in both (upstream), so that an equal count with different members is not read as parity; keeps a committed allowlist of files out of scope (precompile, loading, llvmcall*, threads, ccall to user libraries, spawn, cmdlineargs, compiler, jit), each with a reason, and reports the pass rate per remaining file; stores every failure found only in the interpreter as a regression test once it is fixed. The differential oracles of each stage (M1 Expr, M2 CodeInfo, Random streams, printed show output) are stronger than the suite for the front end and are built first, which is why M0 comes before everything else.

data.scope-of-the-first-version#Scope of the:
In: all syntax JuliaSyntax parses; functions and multiple dispatch with parametric methods and where; keyword arguments; closures; struct and mutable struct; abstract and parametric types; Union, Nothing and Missing; tuples and named tuples; try/catch/finally; hygienic macros and @generated functions; string interpolation; broadcasting; comprehensions and generators; do blocks; modules; using and import of in-image modules; single-threaded tasks and Channel. From the standard library: LinearAlgebra (dense, over go-ndarray), Statistics, Random, Printf, Dates and Test. SparseArrays comes later.
Out: ccall to arbitrary user libraries (an error naming the symbol), llvmcall, @cfunction, parallel Threads.@threads (runs serially), Distributed, Pkg (packages ship in the image), and precompilation of user code.

data: Status: planned (milestones M3 to M5); M3 is in progress. This page counts what Julia’s Base asks of its runtime, and says which fleet library is meant to answer each part. Of it, only the type system is implemented so far: the core package (v0.3.0) holds Julia’s type objects, apply_type and subtyping.
data.builtins-63-in-julia-1126#Builtins: 63 i: julia 1.12.6 has 63 builtins; the bibliography counted 83 on julia 1.15-DEV sources. From src/builtin_proto.h: getfield, setfield!, isa, ===, <:, apply_type, _apply_iterate, invoke, memorynew, the twelve memoryref*, the fourteen *global*, _structtype, _typebody! and the rest. Each is one Go function.
data.ccall-and-ccall-in-base-896-call-sites-i:
856 ccall and 40 @ccall, plus 24 cglobal(. By target:
Target Sites Go implementation Julia runtime jl_*, ios_* 524 (387 unique names) is the Go runtime: reflection, IdDict, strings, files, GC; no-ops or errors for compiler, precompile and CPU-feature calls libc and OS symbols 88 Go os, syscall and time; memcpy and friends on Go slices; malloc and free on a Go arena MPFR 81 static, plus 29 generated go-bignum’s bigfloat and math/big.Float; mpfr_asprintf and mpfr_snprintf need a Go formatter libuv uv_* 78 Go os, os/exec, net and time.Timer; the event loop becomes goroutines that wake the scheduler GMP 40 named, plus 3 interpolated math/big.Int and big.Rat, following GMP’s truncating, floor and ceiling rounding for quotients; go-bignum for factorial and binomial other dynamic (pointer, @static, interpolated) 7 resolved case by case PCRE2 18 see Regex below utf8proc 15 Go unicode and golang.org/x/text/unicode/norm; width and grapheme tables generated from the Unicode version pinned by utf8proc Windows-only and macOS libproc 13 not on WebAssembly; GOOS=windows later libm 0 nothing: Base’s elementary functions are written in Julia over intrinsics, so results are bit-identical by construction The standard libraries read (Random, Dates, Printf, Statistics) have 14 sites: 7 on libdSFMT in Random (the MersenneTwister generator; the default Xoshiro is pure Julia), 3 on MPFR (mpfr_snprintf in Printf, two mpfr_sub_* in Random), 1 on libuv in Dates, and 1 on the runtime. Statistics has 0.
data.fft#FFT: Julia’s Base and standard library have no FFT (no FFTW in base/, stdlib/ or deps/; FFTW.jl is a registry package). A go-julia-fftw package presenting the FFTW.jl and AbstractFFTs.jl API over go-fft is the port, and it is not part of the VM.
data.intrinsics-93-in-julia-1126#Intrinsics::
julia 1.12.6, the release the port follows, has 93 intrinsics. The breakdown below is the bibliography’s, counted on julia 1.15-DEV sources, which have 94: 81 ADD_I, 12 ALIAS and 1 ADD_HIDDEN in src/intrinsics.h. By group (1.15-DEV):
Group Count wrap (bitcast) 1 arithmetic 17 fast arithmetic (aliases) 7 comparisons 15 bitwise 11 conversion 9 checked arithmetic 10 functions (abs_float, copysign_float, sqrt_llvm, …) 9 pointer arithmetic 2 pointer access 2 pointer atomics 6 C interface (cglobal, llvmcall) 2 CPU tests (have_fma, cpu_supports) 2 hidden (cglobal_auto) 1 All except llvmcall and the pointer group map to Go in a few lines each, with math/bits and math. Int128 needs a two-word type, and Float16 and BFloat16 are converted in software. muladd_float is computed as a fused multiply-add, and that choice is documented. pointerref, pointerset and the atomics work on the Go-side byte storage of Memory and Ref: there is no raw address space. llvmcall is not supported: Base has 0 llvmcall( sites.
data.linearalgebra-194-sites#LinearAlgebra: 1: 182 call BLAS or LAPACK through libblastrampoline, inside loops over element types (blas.jl 38, lapack.jl 144: 105 distinct callee expressions), 9 sites over 8 lbt_* names, and 3 sysctlbyname. The mapping is to implement the Fortran BLAS and LAPACK interface of each routine family as Go functions over go-ndarray’s linalg (LU, QR, Cholesky, SVD, Eig, Eigh and least squares exist there), on the column-major Memory{Float64} buffer a Julia Matrix owns, without copying. Families go-ndarray lacks (generalized Schur, banded and tridiagonal factorisations, Bunch-Kaufman) are missing kernels to add to go-ndarray, not to the VM.
data.naming-of-the-packages-around-the-vm#Nam: The plan’s naming mirrors go-embedded-ruby: go-embedded-julia/julia for the VM, with docs, the landing and brand; go-julia- organisations for ports of Julia packages that are not part of the image’s standard library (FFTW, SparseArrays, DataFrames, Distributions, SpecialFunctions); and go-scikit/julia for the go-scikit bindings. A go-julia-* package is Julia code run by the VM plus Go kernels imported from the go-scikit libraries, never a second Go implementation of the same algorithm.
data.regex#Regex: base/regex.jl has PCRE2 semantics. The fleet’s engine is go-ruby-regexp, a pure-Go backtracking VM reimplementing Onigmo. PCRE2 and Onigmo differ in syntax corners (\K, (*VERB)s, callouts, variable-length lookbehind, \h, option letters). The plan is a PCRE2 syntax front end that compiles to the same VM, with test/regex.jl as the oracle and the 18 pcre2_* names implemented on it. If the VM cannot take a construct, the interpreter raises Julia’s ErrorException("PCRE compilation error: …") rather than match differently.
